extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, natural philosophers, and students of classical mechanics and geometric construction (readers of Newton/Principia-style geometry)
extracted.subtask_description: Classical geometric constructions and lemmas for describing conic trajectories (parabola, ellipse, hyperbola) with given points, tangents, axes, times; methods for transforming figures to simpler forms and finding orbital positions from areas proportional to time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: Preservation of analytic order under coordinate transmutation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a point G touches a conic section and a corresponding point g touches another conic obtained by a coordinate scaling/transformation, then the lines touched by G and g are always of the same analytic order. Indeterminates in the equations change dimension consistently under the substitution OA×AB÷ad for AD and OA×dg÷ad for DG, so transformed equations designate lines of the same analytic order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains algebraic substitution to effect coordinate change and argues that unknowns in the transformed equation ascend to the same number of dimensions as in the original, hence tangency/order properties are preserved. Use this when transmuting a given figure to a simpler figure (e.g., making converging lines parallel) before solving a problem; then invert the transformation to obtain the solution in the original figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: Translation preserves tangency (translated tangents are tangents)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line tangents a curved line in one figure, the translated straight line tangents the translated curved line in the transformed figure, and conversely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to transfer tangency relations between original and transformed figures. Useful for reducing problems by translating or otherwise transforming a figure so that known constructive methods apply; proofs can be given geometrically but are presented succinctly here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: Use of figure transmutation to simplify constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: By choosing an appropriate line as the first ordinate (e.g., any straight line through the concurrence of converging lines), converging lines can be transmuted into parallel lines; after solving the problem in the transformed (simpler) figure, inverse operations yield the solution in the original figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this Lemma when a construction is difficult in the original configuration: pick a transformation (affine-type scaling around a point or sending a point to infinity) that simplifies concurrency/parallelism, construct the desired elements in the simpler figure, and then invert the transformation. Particularly useful for problems involving tangents and contact points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXV (Prob. XVII): Trajectory through two given points and tangent to three given lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct the conic trajectory that passes through two given points and is tangent to three given straight lines in given positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: choose two tangent lines so that in the transformed figure they become parallel, use a third tangent to become parallel to the line through the two given points, form parallelogram(s), determine contact points c, d, e via proportional constructions (square/rectangle relations from conic properties), then apply the inverse of the prior transmutation to transfer those contact points back to the original figure. Restriction: the two given points must both lie either between or outside certain limiting tangency points; if one lies between and the other outside, the problem is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXVI (Prob. XVIII): Trajectory through a given point and tangent to four given lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct the conic trajectory that passes through a given point and is tangent to four given lines in given positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take intersections of pairs of tangents and draw a line through the common intersections; apply the transmutation (as in previous Lemma) making two tangents parallel, yielding a new figure where two tangents become parallel. In the new figure find the second point through which the conic must pass (using the figure's center and symmetry); inverse-transform yields two points in the original figure and the previous Proposition (two points + three tangents) constructs the trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXIII: Locating point K on a given position line from ratio data
rubrics_metrics.description: If lines AC and BD terminate at given points A and B and have a given ratio to each other, and the join CD is cut in a given ratio at K, then the point K is located on a given position line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: let AC and BD meet at E; on BE take BG proportional to AE as BD:AC; choose FD equal to EG to set up similar triangles and parallelogram ELKH to place K on the given position line HK. Useful when one must place an intersection point with a specified division ratio on a prescribed line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXIV: Mean proportional semidiameter for two parallel tangents and third tangent
rubrics_metrics.description: If three lines tangent to a conic are given, two of which are parallel and have given positions, then the semidiameter of the conic parallel to those two is the mean proportional between the segments of those two tangents intercepted between their contact points and the third tangent's contact point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let AF and BG be the two given parallel tangents; let EF be the third tangent meeting them. Then the semidiameter CD parallel to AF and BG satisfies AF : CD :: CD : BG (continually proportional). Proof uses conjugate diameters and parallelogram completion. Corollaries give proportional relations for intersections and centers, and concurrency properties of certain lines through contact points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXV: Abscissa relations for parallelogram sides tangent to a conic
rubrics_metrics.description: If the four (infinitely extended) sides of a parallelogram touch a conic section and are cut by a fifth tangent, and abscissae (measured from opposite angles) are taken on the sides, then the abscissa of one side to that side is as the contiguous portion of the adjacent side between the contact point and the third side is to the abscissa of that adjacent side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives proportional relations between segments and abscissae of sides of parallelograms tangent to a conic; corollaries show equality of certain rectangles and relations under further tangent constructions. Use when deducing proportional measurements in tangent- parallelogram configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to Lemma XXV: rectangle equalities and center/bisection properties
rubrics_metrics.description: From Lemma XXV follow: (1) equality of certain rectangles formed from abscissae and side segments; (2) if a sixth tangent is drawn, those rectangles maintain equality under analogous constructions; (3) if certain chords are bisected and a line through the midpoints is drawn, it passes through the center of the conic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These corollaries are practical: they allow one to compute or deduce centers and equal-area rectangles in tangential parallelogram configurations, helpful in constructing centers or other characteristic points of the conic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXVII (Prob. XIX): Trajectory tangent to five given lines (five tangents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct the conic trajectory tangent to five given lines in given positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: assemble quadrilaterals under any four tangents so that their diagonals bisect; the lines through the bisectors of diagonals concur at the center O. Draw a line through O parallel to a chosen tangent at an appropriate distance to touch the desired trajectory. Use parallellization and intersection constructions derived from prior lemmas to find contact points and complete the conic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium: Handling centers or asymptotes given; finding axes and umbilici
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems where centers or asymptotes are given reduce to previous constructions: asymptotes are treated as tangents with their contact points at infinity. Once a trajectory is described, axes and umbilici can be found by constructing certain circles through intersections of moving angle arms and measuring normals from the center to these loci; axes are located by examining where moving crura become parallel or perpendicular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains pragmatic steps for recovering axes and umbilici from an already-constructed trajectory using circle normals, bisectors, and the relationships between angle arms that generated the trajectory. Useful also when asymptotes replace tangents (take contact point at infinity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXVI: Place a triangle of given shape and magnitude with each angle tangent to a corresponding given line
rubrics_metrics.description: Given three lines in specified positions (not all parallel), one can place a triangle of given shape and size so each of its three angles tangents one of the three lines respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: draw three circular segments over the sides of the prescribed triangle, chosen so that their inscribed angles equal the given position-line angles; extend these segments to full circles, find their mutual intersection points, use similarity to position and scale an equal triangle whose angles touch the given lines. Useful for reducing curve-construction problems to placement of similar triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXVIII (Prob. XX): Trajectory equal & similar to given curve with parts intersecting three given lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a trajectory similar and equal to a given curved line DEF such that its parts corresponding to DE and EF are cut by three given position lines AB, AC, BC into segments similar and equal to DE and EF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lemma XXVI to place triangle DEF against the three position lines, then about that triangle describe a trajectory similar to the given curve. This reduces the problem to an earlier triangle placement construction and then drawing the appropriate similar curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXVII: Construct trapezium of given species whose angles are tangent to four given lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Given four position lines (not all parallel and not concurrent), one can construct a trapezium of a given species whose four angles respectively are tangent to these lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: construct three circular segments over the sides of the model trapezium whose inscribed angles correspond to the angle relations of the given lines; extend to full circles, choose points on a constructed line PQ in proportion to given sides, and use similarity to map the model to the given configuration. The detailed construction chooses points on PQ so that proportions AB:BC = PQ:QR etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXIX (Prob. XIX): Trajectory of given species divided by four given lines into ordered proportional parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a trajectory similar to a given curve FGHI so that its parts fg, gh, hi are respectively cut by four given position lines AB&AD, AD&BD, BD&EC in the same order and proportional to FG, GH, HI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a trapezium similar to FGHI whose angles touch the four given lines (via Lemma XXVII), then about that trapezium draw a trajectory similar to the given curve. Alternative constructions (Scholium) involve constructing certain parallels and using angle equalities to produce the trapezium more directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium (to Prop. XXIX): Alternate construction by angle equalities
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative method constructs the required trapezium by extending sides, drawing diagonals and auxiliary lines AK, AL, choosing points so that certain constructed angles equal model angles, and then finishing by circular-arc segment constructions to get the trapezium and the desired trajectory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives an explicit sequence of auxiliary parallels, intersections, and proportion choices leading to the same trapezium as Lemma XXVII; useful when a more algebraic or angle-based construction is desired for practical implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXX (Prob. XXII): Position of a body on a parabolic trajectory at a given time (area proportionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: For motion along a given parabolic trajectory, the area APS (area from vertex to current position bounded by axis and curve) is proportional to time; constructing a circle with center H and radius HS (with GH = 3M where M relates to the area expression) yields intersection P of the parabola giving the body's location after a given time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set 4 × AS × M equal to the area APS (M derived from motion data). Bisect AS at G, erect perpendicular GH such that GH = 3M, then draw circle center H radius HS; its intersection with the parabola yields P. Corollaries: GH : AS equals elapsed time to vertex-to-perpendicular time; velocity ratios follow (point H's velocity to vertex velocity 3:8). Use when motion under inverse-square central force reduces to parabolic segment area proportionality to time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXVIII: Nonexistence of an oval whose area as an abscissa function is finitely expressible
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no oval figure whose area, taken by arbitrary abscissae, can be expressed in generality by an equation with finitely many terms and dimensions. In particular, the area of an ellipse (as a function of abscissa from the umbilicus) cannot generally be given by a finite algebraic equation; therefore some curves are geometrically irrational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses construction of a spiral generated by revolving a line and shows the intersection of that spiral with a line produces infinitely many intersections, hence any finite algebraic equation would have to represent infinitely many roots—impossible. Corollary states that ellipse areas cannot be determined by finite algebraic formulas and so some curves (spirals, quadratrices, trochoids) are 'geometrically irrational'. This justifies the need for non-algebraic (transcendental/series) methods in orbital time-location problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXI (Prob. XXIII): Position on an elliptical trajectory at a given time (trochoid method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an elliptic trajectory with vertex A, umbilicus S, center O, to find the body's location P at a given time, construct a trochoid generated by a wheel of radius equal to circle EFG and relate the trochoid intersection with a line parallel to KG to obtain P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a circle center O with radius OG chosen so OG:OA = OA:OS; roll a wheel (geometrical device) along rule GH to describe a trochoid with base point A; take GK proportional to the arc-time ratio (arc AP : period), erect perpendicular KL to meet the trochoid at L, then draw LP parallel to KG to meet the ellipse at P. Scholium: because exact construction is difficult, practical mechanical approximations and iterative numerical series (convergent rapidly) are recommended; give a stepwise iterative algorithm of small-angle corrections, and special approximations for near-apse positions and for hyperbola analogues. For astronomical use, further simplifications are provided (using angles Y, Z, and successive small corrections V, X etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section VII / Prop. XXXII (Prob. XXIV): Spaces described in rectilinear ascents/descents under inverse-square central force
rubrics_metrics.description: If the centripetal force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the center, then the path described by a body falling along a straight line (not perpendicular) is a conic section whose umbilicus matches the center; spaces described in given times can be determined accordingly (case 1: non-perpendicular fall yields a conic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refers to earlier propositions (XI–XIII) and corollaries establishing the relation between inverse-square central force and conic-motion; to get distances in given times for rectilinear motion, reduce the problem to conic sections and apply the geometrical area/time methods developed earlier for parabolic and elliptic motion.
